newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians, Germans win Russia telecom stake.
newsitem.headline: Russians, Germans win Russia telecom stake.

text.p: A consortium of Russian and German banks won a quarter of Russia's telecoms holding company Svyazinvest on Friday in Moscow's biggest privatisation to date.

The consortium is built around Uneximbank, Russia's third biggest bank headed by youthful ex-cabinet minister Vladimir Potanin, and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG), the London-based investment banking arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank AG .
In Russia's often murky privatisation process, the bidding appeared to have been competitive and the price fair.

Vladimir Malin, deputy chairman of Russia's Federal Property Fund, said the Cyprus-registered Mustcom consortium bid $1.875 billion for 25 percent plus one share in Svyazinvest. It holds controlling stakes in 88 Russian regional and other telecoms firms, including long-distance operator Rostelekom .
The winner must pay the money in instalments over 75 days.
"Ownership rights on the shares will be transferred after full payment, that is after 75 days," Malin said. "After that they can sell these shares or do with them whatever they want."

The bulk of the money goes to the Russian government, which is struggling to pay off billions of dollars in wage arrears. But the deal also opens the way for private investment into Svyazinvest and hence the ramshackle Russian telephone system.
Pinning down just who was behind the winning consortium was complicated.

A spokesman for Uneximbank said it had won the auction with its affiliates, investment bank MFK (ICFI) and Interros Group. Moscow investment bank Renaissance Capital and Deutsche Bank were also in the winning consortium, he said.
Malin said Renaissance, and two other entities, were the owners of Mustcom, and Nick Jordan, managing director of DMG in Moscow, confirmed his bank was part of the group.
He declined to say who else was in Mustcom, saying: "I will leave that to Mr Potanin to describe. He is the head of the consortium."
Uneximbank president Potanin, 36, was first deputy prime minister until President Boris Yeltsin reshuffled the cabinet in March. Uneximbank has already done well out of privatisation.
On behalf of the government, it holds a 38 percent stake in metals group Norilsk Nickel, the world's biggest producer of palladium and possibly nickel by the end of this year.
The Norilsk stake, equivalent to 51 percent of voting shares, is currently being auctioned by Uneximbank, which has said it intends to bid for full ownership.
The Interros Group controlled by Uneximbank also owns most of SIDANKO, Russia's fifth or sixth biggest oil group by output.
The winners of Friday's tender appeared to have paid a fair price, unlike in some previous big sales where a small group of well-connected banks have won with small bids.
The winning bid for Svyazinvest compares with a reserve price of $1.18 billion. A second bidder, Dutch group TeleFAM, offered $1.71 billion.

Russian agencies said TeleFAM had included Spain's Telefonica de Espana SA , Russia's Alfa-Bank and the international investment bank CS First Boston. Industry sources said Russia's Most-Bank may also have participated.

For the government, the sale marks a happy ending to a saga that started in 1995, when the stake was sold to Italy's Stet for about $1.06 billion. That deal soon fell through because of disagreement about the terms.

The federal government, which will get 95 percent of the proceeds of the Svyazinvest sale, will offer another 24 percent stake to Russian investors later this year or next, reducing the state's stake to 51 percent.
Even this first tranche of privatisation will, however, allow Svyazinvest or its subsidiaries to raise funds on the market for much needed investment in infrastructure.
Russia is the world's largest country but even local phone calls, let alone conversations across thousands of kilometres (miles), can be a problematic and often thankless business.

The tender also pointed up the closeness of links in the Russian financial world. DMG's Nick Jordan is the brother of Boris Jordan, chief executive of Renaissance Capital, which has said it will merge with Uneximbank's Bank MFK.
